idiom_name: tonic-build generated *Server trait + *Client over prost/protobuf messages
implementation_notes: tonic-build runs protoc in build.rs and generates a client struct, a server trait and prost message types; the facade is the implementation of the generated service trait whose async methods take Request<PlaceOrderRequest> and return Result<Response<OrderConfirmation>, Status>, while the client calls a cheaply cloneable channel-backed client. The in-crate alternative is a trait-based RPC framework such as tarpc, where a #[tarpc::service] trait is the contract and ordinary serde-typed Rust types are the payload - no .proto and no code-generation step. Use tonic when the peers may not be Rust or when gRPC tooling is required; use a trait-based framework when both ends are Rust and you would rather keep the contract in code.
pitfalls: Blocking or CPU-heavy work inside an async handler starves the runtime; move it to spawn_blocking and keep the handler a thin delegation to the domain.
tonic's default 4MB decode limit fails large coarse responses silently; raise the limit deliberately or return a streaming response instead.
The generated client is cheap to clone but a channel is not: dial once and reuse the endpoint instead of creating a connection per call.

variants.name: tarpc #[service] trait with serde payloads (Rust-only)
variants.implementation_notes: tarpc defines the contract as a Rust trait annotated with #[tarpc::service]: the macro generates the client type and the serve() adapter, request and response types are ordinary Rust types serialised through serde (bincode by default) instead of .proto messages, and Context carries deadlines and trace information with deadline propagation and cascading cancellation. It suits a Rust-only boundary where a schema language would be ceremony, and gives up cross-language clients in exchange.
pitfalls: Serde is the wire format: renamed or reordered fields and a non-self-describing encoding mismatch fail at runtime, not at compile time.
Dropping the request future cancels the server-side work through cascading cancellation, so fire-and-forget must be modelled explicitly.
